title: On‑Prem CP Provisioning Lab Guide and Rollback Notes
content:
Purpose:
This is a hands-on lab guide for provisioning a private control plane (on‑prem / VPC) in a sandbox environment, plus pragmatic rollback and recovery notes. It collects TF module patterns we used in the lab, common failure modes, cutover runway checkpoints, and quick commands for fast remediation during outages.

Scope:
- Initial provisioning of control plane components (seed cluster, controlplane-api, controlplane-db, operator) in an on‑prem test rack or VPC sandbox.
- Upgrade/cutover path from PT (pre-prod) to staging then to prod-like environment.
- Node rotation and surge scaling experiments.
- Rollback recipes for failed upgrades and network flaps.

Assumptions / prerequisites:
- Access: operator@redwood with bastion ssh + kubeconfig for seed cluster.
- Terraform state backend: remote S3-compatible bucket + locking (consul/pg).
- Image registry access and an image promotion tag scheme: cp:v1.2.3 -> cp:v1.2.4-canary -> cp:v1.2.4
- KMS/HSM keys already injected into vault for KMS integration.
- Observability hooks: metrics exported to Prometheus pushgateway and tracing to Jaeger.

Lab topology (quick):
- seed-cluster (3 x m5.large equiv) running bootstrap operator
- controlplane-api (2 replicas) behind metal LB (keepalived or f5)
- controlplane-db (primary + replica in same rack) – Postgres with synchronous commit in lab
- operator (deploys model-serving agents) in a separate namespace

TF module patterns we tested (notes + rationale):
- module naming: "cp-*" prefix, separate modules for networking, db, api, operator. Keeps plans small.
- inputs to expose: cluster_id, region_tag, service_cidr, allowed_admin_cidrs, uptime_policy.
- outputs to rely on: api_lb_ip, db_replica_ips (list), kms_key_id, tf_state_lock_key.

Idempotency hints:
- Use local-exec guards: only run bootstrap scripts when a tag file is missing on instance (eg /var/lib/cp-bootstrap.done).
- For resources with non-deterministic names (cloud-init created), add lifecycle ignore_changes for user_data or metadata keys that change frequently.
- Enable plan-only CI on PRs: terraform plan with -out and automated drift job nightly.

Module upgrade pattern (safe-by-default):
1) Build image and tag with canary label. Push to registry and create GitHub PR to terraform-modules referencing new image.
2) Apply to sandbox with terraform apply -target=module.cp_api -auto-approve.
3) Smoke: hit /healthz, check metrics for error spikes, drain one replica and hit fallback routes.
4) Promote to staging (apply entire stack). Wait 30–60m.
5) When staging stable, do a rolling deploy to prod with maxUnavailable=1 and canary traffic 5–10% for 15 minutes.

Cutover checklist (runway):
- Precutover (T-48h): verify state backups (tfstate + pgdump), confirm KMS rotation window, assign oncall.
- T-12h: run terraform plan in staging and export plan artifact.
- T-2h: ensure metrics alert thresholds disabled for non-critical alerts, trace retention increased for 24h.
- T-15m: switch traffic to canary LB, mark feature flag off for auto-fallbacks.
- Postcutover (+1h): run smoke tests and run a full traffic replay for representative prompts.

Node rotation and surge scaling recipe:
- Rotation: drain -> cordon -> wait for steady-state pods to reschedule (watch HPA and PV attachments). Use: kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data --timeout=20m.
- If PVCs fail to reattach, check storage controller logs; for local PVs, prefer a controlled maintenance window.
- Surge scaling: change autoscaler target (or bump machinepool count) and watch queue length; rollback if latency > 2x baseline for 10m.

Quick rollback playbook (fastest path):
1) If controlplane-api upgrade causes errors: revert image tag in tf module and apply module.api with -target to quickly roll back.
2) If DB migration fails: restore latest pgdump to a warm standby node, redirect api to standby by changing api_lb backend weights.
3) If network partition: re-enable cross-rack routes or failover to DR site (DNS TTL considerations).
4) If instance bootstrapping fails due to cloud-init: reprovision with previous AMI and ensure /var/lib/cp-bootstrap.done present.

Common failure modes observed in the lab (with mitigation):
- TF apply hung due to state lock: use lock holder lookup (consul/pg) and force-unlock only after confirming no concurrent operator.
- Pod stuck in ContainerCreating due to CSI attach: scale down and reschedule on different node; check kubelet logs for attach errors.
- LB healthcheck misconfigured after API change: rollback API change and update LB health route to /healthz-v2.

Operational commands (cheat sheet):
- terraform workspace select sandbox && terraform plan -out plan.sbx
- terraform apply -target=module.cp_api -auto-approve
- kubectl -n cp get pods -o wide
- kubectl drain node-03 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data --force
- psql -h cp-db-primary -U rcpadmin -c "SELECT now(), pg_is_in_recovery();"

Smoke test checklist (automated):
- /v1/ping returns 200 within 100ms
- Token auth flows succeed for 10 test tokens
- KV cache hit rate > 70% after 2 minutes of warmup
- End-to-end sample generation latency within baseline +- 25%

Open questions / TODOs (lab findings):
- Investigate using dual-writer DB pattern during migrations to reduce failover time.
- Formalize TF module version policy (semver vs. commit-hash pinning) for private customers.
- Add a preflight job that simulates heavy prefix cache pressure to validate batching heuristics at scale.

Appendix: short terraform snippet we used for safe canary rollout (example):

# module cp_api usage (pseudo)
# module "cp_api" {
#   source = "../../modules/cp_api"
#   image_tag = var.image_tag
#   replicas  = var.replicas
#   lb_health_path = "/healthz"
# }

Notes: this doc is intentionally a lab‑oriented, informal playbook — copy relevant sections into the formal runbook when we validate them in two consecutive cutovers. If you take this guide into the field, please update linked_artifacts and add retrospective notes under the Confluence ID above.
